title: A volcano that breathes
subtitle: Kīlauea, Hawaiʻi

technical.title: LOS displacement at Kīlauea summit, NISAR pair 2026-08-18 to 2026-08-30
technical.subtitle: NISAR L2 GUNW (provisional), track 72 descending, tilt removed by Aevion
technical.summary: Line-of-sight displacement from a NISAR L-band (λ = 24.2 cm) interferogram with a 12-day baseline spanning Episode 54 (USGS HVO). Unwrapped phase converted to meters, referenced to the median of high-coherence cells, then a quadratic surface fitted to cells more than 9 km from the vent was removed to take out atmospheric and orbital tilt. Shown at about 120 to 135 m per cell in the story grid (reduced from the 80 m product). One geometry cannot separate vertical from horizontal motion.
caveats: The source interferogram is a provisional NISAR product, not validated by NASA.
The sign convention (positive = away from the satellite) is assumed from the phase-to-range relation and has not been checked against NISAR documentation.
A smooth quadratic tilt was removed using cells more than 9 km from the vent. This can also remove real broad deformation, so only the local pattern should be read.
Coherence is only about 0.5 on average (forest and old lava), so fine detail is uncertain. The area near the vent has no data.

The pair also spans other changes between Aug 18 and Aug 30. The next pair (Aug 30 to Sep 11) has no eruption and shows the opposite sign at the same place. That is consistent with the summit sinking during the eruption and swelling back afterward, but this is an interpretation to confirm.
The eruption time comes from a summary of the USGS HVO timeline and must be checked on the HVO page before it is shown as fact.

dataStatusNote: Ground motion is measured by NISAR (provisional L2 GUNW interferogram, track 72 descending, Aug 18 to Aug 30, 2026), read and tilt-corrected by Aevion. It is not validated by NASA. The eruption time comes from the USGS HVO timeline and still needs checking against the HVO page.

storyText: Kīlauea is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth, and in 2026 it erupted about every two weeks. NISAR flew over on August 18 and again on August 30, with a nine-hour lava fountaining episode in between. Comparing the two radar passes shows how the ground around the summit moved, in this measurement from NISAR.

why.title: Why does the ground move at a volcano?
why.body: Magma collects in a reservoir a kilometer or two under the summit. As it fills, the ground above bulges outward. When the magma erupts or drains away, the ground sinks back. The changes are small, often a few centimeters, but radar can see them across the whole volcano.

why.title: How does radar see it?
why.body: NISAR sends L-band radar pulses and records the echo. Comparing two passes 12 days apart, a tiny change in distance to the ground shifts the echo's phase. One full color cycle in the Fringes view is about 12 cm of motion toward or away from the satellite.

why.title: Why can radar struggle here?
why.body: Fresh lava, ash and dense rainforest scramble the echo, so some areas have no usable data. L-band, which NISAR uses, keeps signal through vegetation better than shorter wavelengths, but the area right around a vent can still drop out.

why.title: What does this help with?
why.body: Scientists at the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory combine ground measurements like these with gas, seismic and GPS data to judge when magma is on the move. Satellite radar fills the gaps between instruments.

tour.title: Kīlauea
tour.text: This is the summit of Kīlauea on the Island of Hawaiʻi. The crater in the middle is Halemaʻumaʻu.

tour.title: NISAR looks once
tour.text: On August 18, 2026, NISAR passes over and records the ground. This is the "before" picture.

tour.title: The volcano erupts
tour.text: On August 25, lava fountains erupted from the summit for about 9 hours (Episode 54, per the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory timeline). Magma leaving the shallow reservoir makes the ground above it change shape.

tour.title: NISAR looks again
tour.text: On August 30, NISAR flew over again. Comparing the two passes shows how the ground moved. Orange means away from the satellite, blue means toward it.

tour.title: The summit moved
tour.text: Around the summit caldera, the ground moved away from the satellite (orange) at the vent by about 4 cm, and toward it (blue) to the east by about 4 cm. The blank patch is where lava and the caldera scrambled the radar.

tour.title: Counting the waves
tour.text: Each color band is about 12 cm of motion. Tight rings around the summit mean the ground changed a lot there.

tour.title: How sure are we?
tour.text: Dark areas have gaps in the data, often right at the vent where fresh rock and ash scramble the radar. We hide what we cannot trust.

layers.name: Ground motion (line of sight)
layers.hintStory: Orange means the ground moved away from the satellite, blue means toward it. Changes under 1.5 cm are left clear so the real motion stands out. Around the summit it reaches about 4 cm.
layers.hintScientist: LOS displacement in meters after referencing and tilt removal. Positive = away from the satellite (assumed, not verified). Changes below 15 mm are drawn transparent. Cells near the vent have no data.

provenance.measurement: Radar line-of-sight displacement, relative to a reference level
provenance.signConvention: Positive = away from the satellite (range increase). Assumed from the phase-to-range relation; not verified against NISAR documentation.
provenance.geometry: Track 72 descending, frame 79, HH, left-looking, about 39 degrees from vertical (typical; confirm from the granule)
provenance.method: Aevion read unwrappedPhase inside the map box, set invalid cells (connected component 0) to no data, converted phase to meters, subtracted the median of cells with coherence above 0.8, resampled to a 220 by 200 grid, then removed a robust quadratic surface fitted to cells with coherence of at least 0.3 beyond 9 km of the vent.
provenance.license: NASA data, free to use. Research-grade, not for operational use.

layers.label: Coherence
layers.name: Coherence
layers.titleStory: How much we can trust it
layers.hintStory: Bright means the two radar passes matched well. Dark means the ground or plants changed too much to trust the measurement. The blank patch is where radar returned no usable signal.
layers.hintScientist: Interferometric coherence magnitude from the GUNW product, 0 to 1. Mean about 0.5. Cells below the threshold are faded and hatched when masking is on.

provenance.method: Same box, resampling and invalid mask as the displacement layer.
